items.s: The rep must understand the product and believe it is suitable for at least some investors.
items.w: Reasonable-basis suitability is about product understanding and suitability for at least some investors, not one client.

items.s: A fraud or manipulative device fails this test no matter who the client is.
items.w: A fraudulent or manipulative product cannot be suitable for anyone, so it fails the reasonable-basis test outright.

items.s: It focuses on the rep’s understanding of the product rather than on any individual customer.
items.w: The book says reasonable-basis suitability does not consider each customer individually but the rep’s product knowledge.

items.s: A rep recommends a product she does not fully understand, so this test is failed.
items.w: Recommending a product without understanding its features fails the reasonable-basis test according to the chapter.

items.s: The rep must analyze the client’s financial situation and investment profile before recommending.
items.w: Customer-specific suitability requires analyzing a broad array of factors, including the client’s financial situation.

items.s: An institution that affirmatively exercises independent judgment may be exempt from this obligation.
items.w: The institutional account exemption relieves only the customer-specific obligation, when two stated criteria are satisfied.

items.s: It asks whether a recommendation fits one particular institutional customer.
items.w: Customer-specific suitability looks at the particular institutional customer’s profile, unlike the product-level reasonable-basis test.

items.s: A product that is suitable for some investors can still fail this test for the particular client at hand.
items.w: Customer-specific suitability requires the product to be suitable for the specific client, beyond being suitable for someone.

title: FINRA Suitability vs Regulation Best Interest

items.s: Recommendations to institutional customers are judged under this standard.
items.w: Rule 2111 suitability applies to institutional customers, while recommendations to retail customers fall under Reg BI.

items.s: It is composed of reasonable-basis, customer-specific and quantitative suitability obligations.
items.w: Those three obligations make up the Rule 2111 suitability analysis and must each be met on every recommendation.

items.s: A recommendation must fall within the zone of what is appropriate for the customer.
items.w: The chapter contrasts suitability’s zone of what is appropriate with Reg BI’s higher best-interest standard.

items.s: This standard is set by FINRA rather than adopted by the SEC.
items.w: Rule 2111 is FINRA’s suitability rule, whereas Regulation Best Interest was passed by the SEC.

items.s: The SEC passed it in 2019 to enhance protection for retail investors.
items.w: Regulation Best Interest was passed by the SEC in 2019 to raise standards of retail investor protection.

items.s: The customer’s interests must be placed ahead of the firm’s and the representative’s interests.
items.w: Putting the customer’s interests ahead of the firm and rep is the heightened standard Reg BI established.

items.s: A customer relationship summary must be provided at or prior to the recommendation.
items.w: Form CRS delivery at or before the recommendation is part of the Reg BI disclosure obligation.

items.s: Its four obligations are disclosure, care, conflict of interest and compliance.
items.w: Reg BI firms must address disclosure, care, conflict of interest and compliance obligations as listed in the chapter.

items.s: The issuer buys back the security when interest rates fall in order to reissue at lower rates.
items.w: Call risk is the issuer exercising its call feature in falling rate environments to re-issue cheaper securities.

items.s: Callable bonds and callable preferred stock are the investments most at risk.
items.w: The chapter names callable bonds and callable preferred stock as the investments most exposed to call risk.

items.s: Purchasing non-callable securities mitigates this risk.
items.w: Non-callable securities cannot be redeemed early by the issuer, which is the strategy listed to reduce call risk.

items.s: Call protection prevents the issuer from redeeming the security for a set period.
items.w: Call protection bars the issuer from calling the security for a certain period, which protects bondholders.

items.s: Homeowners refinance to a lower rate and return principal to the holders early.
items.w: Mortgage refinancing in falling rate environments gives MBS holders an early return of principal, which is prepayment risk.

items.s: Mortgage-backed securities are the investments most at risk.
items.w: Prepayment risk is distinctly linked to mortgage-backed securities, which the chapter lists as most at risk.

items.s: Investing in other fixed-income securities and equities mitigates this risk.
items.w: The listed strategy for prepayment risk is investing in other types of fixed-income securities and in equities.

items.s: A recession or war that pushes down the overall market is an example.
items.w: Recessions, wars and significant political events are named sources of systematic, market-wide risk.

items.s: It cannot be avoided through diversification but can be hedged with derivatives such as options.

items.s: Buying put options on a broad-based index is the listed strategy to mitigate it.
items.w: Puts on a broad index are the strategy given for hedging market-wide systematic risk in the chapter.

items.s: For owners of stocks, it is highest in a falling bear market.

items.s: It is also called business risk and generally does not affect the investor’s entire portfolio.
items.w: Non-systematic risk is also called business risk and does not usually hit every holding in a portfolio.

items.s: A product recall or a management change at a single company is an example.
items.w: Company-specific events such as recalls and management changes are the chapter’s examples of non-systematic risk.

items.s: The best protection is diversifying across many individual stocks or broad-based funds.
items.w: Diversification is the best protection against non-systematic risk because no one position dominates the portfolio.

items.s: Volkswagen’s emissions scandal, which hurt one company’s stock, is a typical example.

title: Inflationary Risk vs Interest Rate Risk

items.s: It is also known as purchasing power risk.
items.w: The chapter states inflationary risk is also referred to as purchasing power risk.

items.s: A fixed coupon stays the same while the cost of goods and services rises.
items.w: Fixed payments buy less over time when prices rise, which is the essence of inflationary risk.

items.s: Investing in TIPS and REITs is a listed way to reduce it.
items.w: TIPS, REITs and common stock are the strategies the chapter lists for mitigating inflationary risk.

items.s: The return of par at maturity buys fewer real goods because prices have risen.
items.w: The chapter notes the returned principal at maturity has reduced purchasing power in an inflationary environment.

items.s: Bond prices fall when rates rise, because of the inverse relationship between prices and rates.
items.w: The inverse price and rate relationship is the definition of interest rate risk for fixed-income securities.

items.s: Bonds with a lower coupon and longer maturity are especially exposed.
items.w: The Knopman Note says lower coupon and longer maturity bonds are especially exposed to interest rate risk.

items.s: Compared with credit or political risk, an investor buying Treasury securities is most concerned with this one.
items.w: Treasuries have little credit or political risk, so the buyer’s main concern is interest rate risk.

items.s: Investing in convertible bonds is a listed way to reduce it.
items.w: Convertible bonds, along with common stock, are the strategies listed for mitigating interest rate risk in the chapter.

items.w: The chapter lists fixed-income and preferred stock as inappropriate for a pure growth objective.

items.s: Its biggest risks are market risk and business risk.
